title: Advanced Pedagogy — An Overview

pts: Discourse analysis studies how language functions above the sentence, in real stretches of speech and writing.
This goes well beyond Tier II's introductory cohesion devices into the structural analysis of whole texts and conversations.
This is the analytical foundation for the genre and pragmatics work that follows in this tier.

v: Two short versions of the same paragraph (see model language)

items: Give pairs two versions of a paragraph with the same sentences, one in a logical order with linking words and one jumbled with the linking words removed.
Ask which is easier to read and why. Collect answers on the board.
Sort the reasons into two columns: ‘words that link’ and ‘ideas that follow’.
Explain that the first column is broadly cohesion and the second coherence, and that both belong to discourse, the level above the sentence.
Pairs repair the weaker version.
Use two spoken exchanges, one natural and one in which each reply ignores the previous turn.
Support: highlight the linking words in the stronger version before learners begin.
Challenge: learners write a version that is cohesive but makes no sense.

blocks.x: Two versions of a paragraph (written for this book):

lines: A: Bengaluru was once known as a city of lakes. Many of them were built centuries ago to store monsoon rain. Today, however, a large number have disappeared under roads and buildings. Those that remain are often polluted, which is why citizen groups have begun to restore them.

B: Citizen groups have begun to restore them. Bengaluru was once known as a city of lakes. A large number have disappeared under roads and buildings. They were built centuries ago to store monsoon rain.
S1: In B, ‘them’ comes first. We don’t know what ‘them’ is.
S2: And A has ‘however’ and ‘which is why’. It shows the reason.

blocks.x: Unit 52 develops cohesion and coherence in full, including reference chains and given-new ordering.

body: Purpose: to show analysis above the sentence. Content: a horizontal line; below it, single sentences with grammar labels; above it, a paragraph with arrows linking pronouns to nouns. Style: clean diagram, two colours plus labels. Board version: a line with ‘sentence’ under it and ‘text’ above it.

items: Google Docs (free) with the highlighter for marking linking words on screen.

blocks.x: Both versions written on the board or on half-sheets of paper.

pts: Pragmatics studies meaning in context — implicature, speech acts, and the gap between literal and intended meaning.
This extends Tier I and II's pragmatics previews (Units 24, 27) into a full analytical and pedagogical framework.
Pragmatic competence is argued to be one of the last aspects of a language non-native speakers fully acquire.

items: Give groups six short exchanges in which the reply does not answer the question literally.
Groups write what each reply really means.
Discuss how they worked it out: from context, relationship or tone.
Groups say how the same meaning would be expressed in their home language, and whether it would be more or less direct.
Learners collect indirect replies they hear at home or in shops, in any language.
Support: offer three possible meanings for each exchange to choose from.
Challenge: learners write a blunter and a more indirect reply, and rank all three.

lines: A: Are you coming to Ravi’s wedding on Sunday?
B: My cousin’s exam is on Monday.
Likely meaning: Probably not; I need to stay home.
A: How was the new restaurant?
B: Well, the parking was easy.
Likely meaning: The food was not good.

blocks.x: The meaning lies in what the listener infers in context, the territory of pragmatics (Leech 1983). Advanced learners often master grammar well before these inferences; Unit 53 treats them in full.

body: Purpose: to show the gap between what is said and meant. Content: an iceberg; above the water, ‘The parking was easy’; below it, context, relationship, shared knowledge and inference. Style: simple, cool colours. Board version: a triangle with a wavy line across it.

items: Mentimeter (free plan, limited questions) to collect anonymous interpretations.

blocks.x: Slips of paper; groups hold up their interpretation on a card.

pts: Building on Tier II's genre awareness, this develops a complete cycle for teaching learners to produce whole genres independently.
The teaching-learning cycle moves from deconstruction to joint construction to independent construction.
This is one of the most well-evidenced approaches to teaching academic and professional writing.

v: One writing task from your syllabus

items: Choose a writing task you will teach this term, such as a formal complaint or a report.
Draw four boxes: building the field, deconstruction, joint construction, independent construction.
In each box, note one activity you could use for this genre.
Mark the stage you usually skip. For many teachers it is joint construction.
Plan ten minutes of joint construction for your next writing lesson.
DIET faculty run this with trainee teachers, each planning a different genre.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A sketch plan for a formal letter of complaint to a municipal office (written for this book):

lines: Building the field: discuss a real local problem, such as irregular water supply.
Deconstruction: label the moves in a model letter: situation, problem, effect, request, closing.
Joint construction: the teacher writes as the class suggests sentences, thinking aloud about tone.
Independent construction: each learner writes about a different problem.

blocks.x: The Sydney School cycle reduces support stage by stage (Martin and Rose 2008). Unit 54 describes it in full, building on the genre awareness of Unit 33.

body: Purpose: to show gradual release across the cycle. Content: four panels; in the first the teacher holds a large pen, in the last the learner holds it alone. Style: warm, simple figures. Board version: four boxes with a pen moving from teacher to learner.

items: Google Slides (free) to display the model text and annotate moves.

blocks.x: The four-box plan drawn in the teaching journal.

pts: Tier II introduced CLIL as an occasional lesson; this tier develops full content-and-language-integrated course design.
This includes sustained collaboration models, assessment across both content and language, and materials development at scale.
CLIL at this depth typically requires institutional commitment, not just individual teacher enthusiasm.

v: A science or social science chapter; the CLIL lesson from Unit 37

items: Take a CLIL lesson you have taught, or the water-cycle lesson in Unit 26.
With a subject colleague, list the content outcomes of its whole chapter.
Sketch the chapter as a sequence of lessons, each with a content aim and a language aim.
Note the institutional support you would need: shared planning time, materials, agreement on assessment.
Where one teacher teaches both subjects, sketch the plan alone but in two colours, one for content and one for language.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Four lessons for a Class 8 chapter on crop production (written for this book):

lines: L1 Kharif and rabi crops: content: seasons; language: comparing (‘whereas’).
L2 Preparing the soil: content: tools and steps; language: sequencing and the passive.
L3 Irrigation methods: content: traditional and modern; language: advantages and disadvantages.
L4 Report: a group report on a crop grown in the learners’ district.

blocks.x: Unit 55 shows how to plan such a unit with the 4Cs framework (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010) and how to assess content and language separately.

body: Purpose: to contrast light-touch and full CLIL. Content: a single brick labelled ‘one lesson’ beside a small wall whose mortar is labelled ‘collaboration’, ‘materials’ and ‘assessment’. Style: simple, earthy colours. Board version: one box beside four joined boxes.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for textbook-linked videos and diagrams in several languages.

blocks.x: The chapter and a planning sheet shared between the two teachers.

pts: Building on Tier II's autonomy-in-practice work, this tier addresses learners capable of largely self-directed study.
Learning contracts and self-access systems formalise autonomy into a structured, sustainable practice.
This level of autonomy is realistic for many C1 learners in ways it typically isn't at lower proficiency levels.

items: Ask learners to name one area of English they want to improve in the next four weeks.
Help them turn it into a specific goal with a measurable outcome.
Each learner chooses resources, a weekly time and a way of showing progress.
Learners sign the contract; the teacher countersigns.
Review progress in a five-minute weekly conference.
Pairs share contracts and act as ‘accountability partners’ between conferences.
Support: offer a menu of goals and resources to choose from.
Challenge: learners design their own way of assessing the outcome.

blocks.x: A learner’s contract (written for this book):

lines: Goal: To give a five-minute talk without notes on a topic from my engineering course.
Resources: two short online talks a week; the library’s presentation guide.
Time: three sessions of 30 minutes a week.
Evidence: a recorded talk in week 4, compared with a recording from week 1.

blocks.x: Holec (1981) defined autonomy as the ability to take charge of one’s own learning; a contract gives that ability a structure. Unit 56 extends the autonomy work of Unit 48 to contracts and self-access systems.

body: Purpose: to show the parts of a learning contract. Content: a one-page document with five labelled sections (goal, resources, time, evidence, review) and two signature lines. Style: clean, like a real form. Board version: five headings in a column.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared contract template that learners copy and complete.

blocks.x: A printed or hand-copied contract kept in the learner’s notebook.

pts: This tier addresses actually designing tests, not just using and interpreting ones already provided.
Deep washback design deliberately engineers a test's backward effect on teaching to be positive.
This is genuinely specialist territory, connecting language testing theory directly to classroom practice.

v: A past examination paper for English

items: List the skills each section of a past paper rewards.
Note what teachers are likely to do in class because of each section.
Identify one section with likely negative washback, such as a memorized letter format.
Redesign one item so that preparing for it would require the kind of teaching you want.
Compare an old board paper with a recent competency-based sample paper.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Original: Write a letter to the editor about the problem of stray dogs in your locality. (Format: 2 marks; content: 3 marks.)
Redesign: Read the two short letters below, which take opposite views. Write a reply to one of them, responding to at least two of its points.

blocks.x: The redesign rewards reading and argument, so it cannot be prepared for by memorizing a model. Hughes (2003) advises testing the abilities we want to encourage, directly where possible. Unit 57 treats washback design in depth.

body: Purpose: to show washback as the test’s influence on earlier teaching. Content: a timeline running from ‘teaching’ to ‘test’, with a curved arrow from the test back to the classroom. Style: clear, one accent colour. Board version: a line with two labels and a curved arrow.

items: Google Forms (free) to trial a redesigned item with a class and see the range of answers.

blocks.x: Photocopies of the past paper; the redesign written on the board.

pts: Building on Tier II's brief corpus mention, this tier develops genuine skill in using corpus tools for teaching decisions.
Concordance analysis, frequency data, and collocation patterns replace intuition with evidence at a much deeper level.
This connects language description directly to materials design and error correction.

v: Access to one free corpus tool, or printed concordance lines

items: Choose a pair of words learners often confuse, such as make and do with nouns.
Ask learners to predict which nouns go with each verb.
Search a corpus tool for each verb and look at the most frequent nouns that follow it.
Compare predictions with the evidence.
Learners write two rules of thumb based on the data, not on the textbook.
Search for a word learners overuse, such as very, and find stronger alternatives.
Support: provide printed concordance lines with the key word in bold.
Challenge: learners compare spoken and written frequencies, where the tool allows.

blocks.x: Predictions and evidence (the corpus lines are summarized, not quoted):

lines: S1: I think ‘do a mistake’ is correct.
T: Let’s look. After make, one of the most frequent nouns is mistake. After do, we find homework, business, research.
S2: So ‘make a mistake’, but ‘do homework’.

blocks.x: A corpus is a large, principled collection of real texts searched with software; concordance lines reveal patterns that intuition misses (Sinclair 1991). Unit 58 develops these skills for materials design and feedback.

body: Purpose: to show what corpus evidence looks like. Content: eight aligned lines of text with the key word make in a central column in bold, and the following nouns highlighted. Style: monospaced text on a light background. Board version: five lines written with the key word lined up.

items: SkELL (free, Sketch Engine for Language Learning) for simple example sentences and collocations.
AntConc (free) for teachers building a small corpus of their own texts.

blocks.x: Concordance lines printed from a teacher’s search and photocopied.

body: A corpus of American or British English will not show which forms are standard in Indian English. Use corpus evidence to inform choices, not as a verdict on local usage (Unit 74).

pts: Language teaching carries ideological weight — whose English, whose norms, whose voices are centred.
Critical language awareness examines these questions explicitly, rather than treating language as a neutral technical system.
This closes the loop on Tier I and II's culture and intercultural competence work with genuinely critical depth.

v: Three short texts about the same event from different sources

items: Give groups three short reports of the same local event, written from different positions (see model language).
Groups note differences in word choice, who is named and what is left out.
Discuss how each text positions the reader.
Ask which variety of English the coursebook presents as ‘correct’, and whose names and places appear in it.
Learners rewrite one sentence to shift its point of view.
Analyse advertisements for coaching institutes and the values they assume.
Support: provide a checklist of features to look for (verbs, labels, quoted voices).
Challenge: learners write a short commentary comparing two texts.

blocks.x: Three headlines about a protest (written for this book):

lines: Farmers block highway, commuters stranded for hours.
Farmers demand fair price for tomatoes in highway protest.
Police clear highway after five-hour agitation.
T: Who is the main actor in each headline?
S1: In the first, the farmers. They cause the problem.
S2: In the third, the police. The farmers are not even named.

blocks.x: Critical language awareness asks learners to notice how language constructs a view of the world (Fairclough 1992). Unit 59 develops this approach, and Units 71 and 74 connect it to multilingualism and World Englishes.

body: Purpose: to show how framing changes what readers see. Content: one highway scene seen through three windows, each labelled with a headline and showing a different part of it. Style: clear, neutral. Board version: three rectangles with a headline over each.

items: Google Docs (free) for side-by-side comparison with comments.

blocks.x: Headlines cut from local English newspapers and pasted on chart paper.

body: Choose the strand your strongest learners need most, teach its activity this month, and note what they found difficult. Keep the note for the Part III checkpoints in Units 60 and 70.

dek: Unit 51 of 100: Tier III opens. Where Tier II integrated the skills, Tier III goes deeper into the discourse, pragmatic, and methodological expertise of a C1-level practitioner.

aims.x: This unit opens Part III. Part I laid the foundations of classroom teaching, and Part II showed how to integrate the skills through tasks, projects, genres and communicative assessment. Part III is for the teacher who is ready to specialize. Like Unit 26, this unit is a map: each point introduces one strand of advanced practice, offers one usable activity, and names the later unit that treats it in full.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what distinguishes advanced pedagogy from the integrated methodology of Part II;
describe discourse analysis and use it to examine a short text;
explain pragmatic meaning and why it is often the last area learners master;
outline the teaching-learning cycle of genre-based writing pedagogy;
distinguish a single CLIL lesson from a full content-and-language unit;
describe how learning contracts formalize autonomy for advanced learners;
explain what it means to design a test for positive washback;
use a free corpus tool to check an intuition, and ask whose English a course presents.

why: Why this matters. Tier II gave every teacher a solid, integrated methodology. Tier III is for the practitioner ready to specialise — in discourse, genre, autonomy, and testing design.

background.x: Teachers who reach this point can usually plan a sound communicative lesson, run a task cycle and assess performance with a rubric. What they often find is that their strongest learners, at B2 and C1, stop improving in ways a coursebook can measure. Grammar is largely accurate and vocabulary wide, yet essays do not quite hang together and requests sound abrupt. The problems have moved above the sentence and into context. Part III is built around that observation.

Two traditions of linguistic description underpin much of what follows. Discourse analysis studies stretches of language longer than a sentence and the ways in which speakers and writers build connected meaning (McCarthy 1991). Pragmatics studies meaning in use: what speakers intend, how listeners infer it, and how social relationships shape choices of form (Leech 1983). Genre theory, especially the Sydney School, has turned description into a teaching cycle (Martin and Rose 2008); corpus linguistics has supplied evidence about real usage (Sinclair 1991); and critical approaches remind us that every choice of model, norm and text says something about whose voices count (Fairclough 1992).

The Indian context gives this tier particular weight. Many learners in Karnataka move between three or more languages in a day and reach advanced English through higher education or work. NEP 2020 asks for multilingual, competency-based education and for critical thinking rather than rote learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 builds language education on the home language and on using language for thinking (NCERT 2023). A learner who can analyse how an editorial positions its reader, write a coherent report and negotiate politely in a meeting is using English as a resource for citizenship and work, not merely as a subject.
The unit is written for experienced teachers, teacher educators and DIET faculty working with learners at B1+ to C1.

items: Discourse repair. Learners restore coherence to a jumbled or poorly linked paragraph and explain two of their changes.
Pragmatic interpretation. Learners explain the intended meaning of three indirect replies and suggest a more or less direct version.
Contract review. A learner’s four-week contract, evidence and short self-evaluation.
Teacher portfolio. A redesigned test item, a genre-cycle plan and a sketch CLIL unit, each with a short rationale.
Where do your strongest learners still struggle, and is the difficulty at sentence level or above it?
When did you last teach what a reply means rather than what it says?
Which stage of the genre cycle do you most often skip, and why?
Which subject colleague would you most like to plan a full content unit with?
Whose English, names and places appear in the materials you use most?

perm: All paragraphs, exchanges, headlines, contracts, plans and test items are written for this book. Corpus lines are summarized rather than reproduced; any concordance lines printed in the book must follow the terms of the corpus provider. Screenshots of Google Docs, Slides or Forms, Mentimeter, DIKSHA, SkELL or AntConc require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: A unit of work in which a subject topic, such as the water cycle, and the English needed to learn it are planned and taught together, using the 4Cs framework.
A list of all the examples of a word or phrase in a corpus, shown with their context and aligned on the key word, used to study patterns of use.
A large, principled collection of real spoken or written texts stored electronically, used to study how language is actually used; plural corpora.
Awareness of how language is used to shape views and maintain power, which language education should help learners develop (Fairclough 1992).

The study of language beyond the sentence: how texts and conversations are organized, how they hang together and how meaning depends on context. It helps teachers explain features such as cohesion, turn-taking and information order.
Meaning that a listener infers beyond what is literally said, based on shared assumptions about cooperative communication (Grice 1975). ‘It’s cold in here’ may imply ‘Please close the window.’
A stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which teacher and class write a text together, with the teacher thinking aloud about the writer’s decisions.

A written agreement, negotiated between learner and teacher, that sets out the learner’s goals, the activities and resources to be used, a timeline and how progress will be evaluated; a brief ‘mini’ version can be built into a single unit.

The study of how meaning depends on context, speakers’ intentions and social relationships, including speech acts, politeness and implied meaning; for example, how ‘It’s cold in here’ can function as a request.
The genre-based cycle of building the field, deconstructing model texts, joint construction and independent construction, with support gradually reduced (Martin and Rose 2008).

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
